title: Home Sweet Home

parts.title: Notices and messages
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: FENWICK GREEN HOUSING: Gas engineers will check all boilers in Block C on Tuesday between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. If nobody will be at home, please leave a key at the office.
LIFT OUT OF ORDER until Friday. Please use the stairs. If you have heavy shopping or a pushchair, ask at the front desk for help.

parts.title: My first flat
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month I moved into my first flat, a small one-bedroom place on the third floor of an old building in Fenwick Green. I had been dreaming about it for years, but the reality was a surprise. On the first night I sat on a box in the empty living room and ate pizza, and I suddenly realised that nobody was going to tell me when to go to bed or when to wash up.

The first week was harder than I had expected. I had a long list of furniture to buy, but the money disappeared quickly: the deposit, the first month's rent and the electricity account. In the end I borrowed a bed from my cousin and found a table on a neighbourhood website for ten pounds. The man upstairs even lent me a drill when I wanted to put up some shelves.

What surprised me most was the silence. I grew up as the only girl in a house with three brothers, so I thought I would love the peace. Instead, I turned on the radio every evening, just to hear voices. Now, a month later, I have started to enjoy my own company, and I have stopped phoning my mum for cooking advice. I am learning to make three dishes properly, and next weekend I am having my first dinner guests. I am nervous, but also excited.

questions.prompt: What did the writer realise on the first night?
options: She had become responsible for herself.
She had forgotten to buy any food.
Her new flat was far too small.
She felt lonely without her brothers.
questions.explanation: She realised that nobody would tell her when to go to bed or wash up, so she was now responsible for herself.

questions.prompt: How did the writer deal with the lack of money?
options: She asked her parents for a loan.
She sold her old furniture at a market.
She used borrowed and cheap furniture.
She waited until she could buy everything new.
questions.explanation: She borrowed a bed from her cousin and bought a ten-pound table on a neighbourhood website.

questions.prompt: What happened with the man upstairs?
options: He asked her to move out.
He complained about the noise she made.
He asked to borrow some of her furniture.
He helped her by lending a tool.
questions.explanation: The man upstairs lent her a drill when she wanted to put up shelves.

questions.prompt: What surprised the writer most?
options: How difficult it was to find furniture.
How many neighbours came to visit.
questions.explanation: She says the silence surprised her most, and she turned on the radio to hear voices.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel now?
options: Lonely and ready to move back home.
Excited because her mother is coming.
Worried about paying for her dinner party.
questions.explanation: A month later she enjoys her own company and is looking forward to cooking for guests.

parts.title: A garage becomes a studio
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
For years, the garage behind our house in Fenwick Green held only bicycles, boxes and a broken washing machine. We never parked a car there because the door was too narrow. [1] Then last winter my mother, who paints in her free time, said she needed a proper place to work.

My father liked the idea at once, and we spent two months turning the garage into a studio. The first job was clearing everything out. [2] We rented a small van to take the old machine to the recycling centre, and we gave the bikes a new home in the shed. After that, my uncle, who is a builder, helped us to fit a large window in the wall facing the garden. [3] But when it was finished, the room filled with natural light, which is exactly what a painter needs.

The walls were painted white, and my father built long shelves for brushes, paper and tins of paint. [4] We found a big wooden table in a charity shop and fixed its broken leg. On the last evening we all stood in the doorway and looked at the finished room. [5] My mother says she has never felt so happy at home, and she now gives painting lessons there every Thursday afternoon.
sentences: It took us three weekends, and we were surprised at how much we had kept.
There was one thing missing, though: a table big enough for large sheets of paper.
Fitting it was difficult, and it took us a whole weekend.
In fact, it had become a place where nobody wanted to look.
My father had always wanted to keep a car there.
She sold her first picture to a neighbour for twenty pounds.
It was hard to believe it was the same place.
Permission from the council was not needed for such a small change.

gaps.explanation: Sentence C explains why nobody used the garage and leads to "Then last winter" when the mother asked for a workplace.
"It took us three weekends" follows the first job of clearing everything out and leads to the van and the old machine.
"Fitting it" refers to the large window, and "But when it was finished" contrasts with the difficult work.
Sentence A introduces the missing table, which the family then finds in a charity shop.
"It was hard to believe it was the same place" follows looking at the finished room, before the mother's reaction. Sentence D is about permission and fits nowhere.

parts.title: Moving house without stress
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Moving to a new home can be stressful, but a good plan makes it easier. Start packing at least a month [1] the move. Begin with things you rarely use, such as books and winter clothes. Write on each box what is [2], so that the movers know where to put it. Remember to [3] the gas and electricity companies about your new address. On moving day, keep the keys, your phone and a few snacks in a bag that stays with you. When the last box has been [4] into the house, do not try to unpack everything at once. First make the beds and find the kettle, because after such a long day you will [5] need a cup of tea. Soon your new house will feel like [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You start packing a month before the move; "until", "since" and "during" do not fit this meaning.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: You write on a box what is inside it; the other prepositions do not make sense here.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "Tell someone about" is correct; "say", "speak" and "talk" cannot be followed directly by "the companies".

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Boxes are carried into a house; they are not painted or dressed.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "You will certainly need a cup of tea" fits; "hardly" and "never" are negative and "already" does not fit a future need.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: "Feel like home" is the fixed expression for feeling comfortable in a place.

parts.title: An email about a new flatmate
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Haruto,
Guess what? We have finally found someone [1] move into the spare room! She is a nurse [2] works at the hospital, [3] she will be out most days, but she will be there at weekends. We met her yesterday, and she seems very friendly. She does not have [4] furniture, only a bed and a desk, so the room will not look crowded. I am a little worried [5] the noise, because she starts work very early. If she has any problem, I hope she will tell us [6] soon as possible. Come and meet her on Sunday!
Bailey

gaps.explanation: "Someone to move in" uses the infinitive with "to" after "someone".
"Who" (or "that") links "a nurse" to what she does.
"So" shows the result: she works at the hospital, so she is out most days.
"Does not have much furniture" is the natural negative with an uncountable noun; "any" also fits.
"As soon as possible" is a fixed expression.

turns.speaker: chidinma

turns.speaker: millie

parts.title: Welcome to a housing co-operative
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: malachy
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Fenwick Green Housing Co-operative. I am Malachy, and I have lived here for nine years. Let me explain how things work. First, our meetings. We hold a meeting on the first Tuesday of every month, at seven in the evening. We used to meet on Thursdays, but too many people played football, so we changed it. The meeting is in the community room, on the ground floor. If the weather is warm, we sometimes go outside to the garden, but the official place is the community room. Now, shared spaces. The laundry is in the basement. You can use the machines from eight in the morning until ten at night, and each wash costs one pound. We don’t have a laundry in the attic any more, because it was too hot. If you have friends or family who want to stay, we have a guest room. It’s very popular. It costs five pounds a night for members’ visitors. For longer visits we have a weekly price, which is twenty-five pounds, but you should ask the committee. For people with bicycles, we have a shed. It is next to the garden, near the back gate. Don’t leave them in the car park, because the cars need the space, and we have had a few thefts there. Finally, the most important thing. A co-operative works because everyone helps. Each member works four hours every month. It could be gardening, cleaning the stairs or helping with paperwork. Some co-ops ask for four hours every week, but we think that’s too much. Please look at the list on the notice board and choose what suits you. Thank you, and welcome again.

gaps.prompt: Monthly meeting: the first ___ at seven
gaps.explanation: They used to meet on Thursdays, but they changed it to the first Tuesday of the month.

gaps.prompt: Meetings are held in the community ___
gaps.explanation: The official place is the community room on the ground floor, not the garden.

gaps.prompt: The shared laundry is in the ___
gaps.explanation: Malachy says the laundry is in the basement; the attic was too hot.

gaps.prompt: The guest room costs five pounds for each ___
gaps.explanation: Visitors pay five pounds a night; the weekly price is twenty-five pounds.

gaps.prompt: The bicycle shed stands beside the ___
gaps.explanation: The shed is next to the garden, near the back gate, and bicycles must not stay in the car park.

gaps.prompt: Every member works four hours each ___
gaps.explanation: Each member works four hours every month, not every week.

parts.title: An interview with an interior designer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Adaeze, you are famous for small flats. What’s the most common mistake that people make?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: Oh, the biggest one is easy. People fall in love with a gorgeous sofa in a shop, buy it, and then it doesn’t fit through the door. Choosing dark colours is a problem too, but you can paint over them. And plants are fine, you can give them away. A sofa is much harder to return. So please measure everything twice.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What first made you interested in small spaces?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: I’m an architect by training, but that’s not it. I didn’t see a television programme either, I hardly watched TV. I grew up in a flat with six people and two rooms. Every corner had a use, and my mother was a genius at it. I think that’s where I learned that small can be beautiful.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: You often say that furniture should have legs. Why?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: It’s a simple trick. If you can see the floor under a table or a sofa, the room feels bigger, because your eye continues under the furniture. It isn’t cheaper, in fact it can cost more, and you have to clean underneath. But the effect is worth it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you recommend about colour?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: Many people want a different colour in each room, and that makes a small flat look cut up. Painting everything white is boring and can feel cold. My advice is to choose colours that are similar, say soft greens and greys, in all the rooms. Then the eye sees one big space.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And where should people keep things they rarely use?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: Not on the kitchen table, obviously, that’s for living. And under the bed is the traditional answer, but then you never see anything again, and it gets dusty. I prefer high shelves. You don’t reach there every day, so it’s perfect for the suitcases and the Christmas decorations.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell us about your last project. How did the couple feel after the work?

turns.speaker: adaeze
turns.text: They are a lovely couple, with a baby, and they were very stressed because of the mess and the noise at home. They never wanted to sell, and the price was reasonable, so no complaints there. When they came back and saw the finished flat, the wife cried and said she felt calmer for the first time in a year.
